Romans made over a hundred of them, at real cost, and never once wrote down why. What was it for?
This is a Roman dodecahedron. And it is one of the strangest objects in all of archaeology.
Today, we'll look at what we actually know, test the most famous theories one by one, and see where a new study from 2025 points.
First, the object itself.
It's made of bronze, or more precisely, a copper alloy.
It has twelve flat faces, each one a perfect pentagon. That's what dodecahedron means: twelve faces.
In the middle of every face, there's a round hole. And here's the strange part: the holes are different sizes.
On every corner, there's a small knob. Twenty corners, twenty knobs.
And the whole thing is hollow.
They come in different sizes. The smallest are about four centimeters across, the biggest about eleven.
The holes range from six millimeters to four centimeters.
The lightest known example weighs about thirty-five grams. The heaviest, about a kilogram.
They were cast using the lost wax technique, and the outsides were finished and probably polished.
Most are decorated, with circles, lines, and dots. The most common pattern is two or three rings carved around each hole.
And the knobs on the corners aren't perfectly identical. That suggests they were made one by one, without a mould, and then soldered onto the body.
One, from Carmarthen in Wales, was cast in a single piece, knobs and all. And one found in London has clusters of three balls on every corner instead of one.
So even within this strange family of objects, no two are quite the same.
This was not a cheap object. It took skill, metal, and time.
And yet, not one of them has a single letter or number on it. No labels. No measurements. No instructions.
Here's another clue: they rarely show signs of wear.
So whatever people did with them, it doesn't seem to have been rough, daily work.
Now, where do they come from?
The first one on record was presented to the Society of Antiquaries of London on the twenty-eighth of June, seventeen thirty-nine. It had been found in a field in Aston, in Hertfordshire, England.
Since then, more than a hundred have been found. One count says a hundred and sixteen. Others say around a hundred and thirty.
They've turned up in Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, and Hungary.
The farthest one to the southeast was found in Serbia. And fragments of two were found in Slovakia, outside the borders of the Roman Empire.
But look at this part of the map. Italy. The heart of the Roman Empire.
Not one has been found there.
Most of them were made in Gaul, roughly modern France and its neighbors, between the second and fourth centuries AD.
And they keep turning up. In 2023, a group of amateur archaeologists found one in excellent condition in the village of Norton Disney, in Lincolnshire, England.
That made thirty-three from Roman Britain alone.
So where exactly were they found?
In Roman military camps. In public baths. In temples, theaters, and tombs. Some were found in hoards of coins. One was found on a riverbed.
Many were found in places where Celtic tribes and Romans met.
But here's the frustrating part. For most of them, we don't know exactly where they came out of the ground.
Many were found long ago, by farmers, collectors, or people digging for something else. The layers of soil around them, which tell archaeologists so much, were never recorded.
So when French archaeologists found one during a proper excavation next to the Roman baths at Jublains, they made it the title of their paper: finally, a dodecahedron in an archaeological context!
And one was found in a tomb, next to a bone object that might have been some kind of handle. But the bone was in such poor condition that it couldn't be excavated and kept.
A handle would change everything. And we lost it.
So we have more than a hundred carefully made objects, spread across the northern part of the empire, found in all kinds of places.
And here's the problem.
The Romans wrote about almost everything. Farming. Building. Medicine. War.
But no description of these objects has ever been found in Roman writing. And no Roman picture shows one.
So researchers have had to guess. And they have guessed a lot.
More than fifty different explanations have been published.
Let's test the most famous ones. Every single one runs into a problem somewhere.
Theory number one: it's a die, for games or for telling the future.
Twelve faces, different holes. You roll it, you read the face that lands on top.
But when people made copies and tried it, the dodecahedrons turned out to be difficult to roll.
Not a great die.
Theory number two: it's a measuring tool.
Physicist Amelia Sparavigna proposed that it worked like a rangefinder. You look through two holes of different sizes, and use them to judge how far away something is.
It's a clever idea. But there's a catch.
A measuring tool usually needs markings, or at least standard sizes. These have no markings, and no two seem to be made to the same standard.
Theory number three, the most famous one online: knitting.
A knitting hobbyist showed that you can wrap wool around the knobs and knit the fingers of a glove, using the different holes for different fingers.
It even works with a modern copy.
But there's no evidence of this kind of knitting until at least a thousand years after these objects were made. The earliest known written reference to spool knitting is from fifteen thirty-five.
And why would anyone cast a knitting tool in polished bronze?
Theory number four: a candle holder.
This one has real physical evidence: traces of wax have been found on some examples.
But a candle holder with twelve holes of different sizes, and knobs on every corner? It explains some of them. Not the design.
Theory number five: a calendar.
The idea is that if you placed a dodecahedron in the right spot, sunlight would line up with two of its holes on a certain day, telling farmers when to plant.
It would explain why they're found mostly in the north of the empire, where the growing season is short.
But nothing on the objects marks a date, a season, or a direction.
And there are more. A gauge to check that coins hadn't been clipped. A masterpiece to prove a metalworker's skill. A child's toy.
Each one fits a few clues. None of them fits all of them.
The coin theory, for example, comes from the coin hoards. If people stored them with their money, maybe they were used to check coins. But then why the knobs? And why twelve different holes?
So let's look at the clues that don't fit any of these theories.
In Germany, near Arloff, archaeologists found a cousin: a bronze icosahedron. Twenty faces instead of twelve, with knobs on the corners, but with holes in only two of its faces.
It's on display in the Rhineland museum in Bonn, right next to two dodecahedrons.
In Geneva, in 1982, a dodecahedron was found made of solid silver.
And in 2009, metal detectorists in France reported something similar but round, a hollow ball with triangular and pentagonal holes.
And much farther away, in Southeast Asia, along old sea trade routes, smaller dodecahedrons made of gold have been found, with the same holes and the same knobs.
So the shape itself seems to have mattered.
And that brings us to the newest idea.
In 2025, two researchers, Michael Guggenberger and Stephen Leach, published a paper in The Antiquaries Journal.
They agree that there is still no description of the object from its own time.
But they argue that several ancient texts point to its possible inspiration, including an overlooked passage in a book called On the Pythagorean Life, by the philosopher Iamblichus.
To the followers of Pythagoras and Plato, the dodecahedron was a shape with deep meaning.
And the authors point to something else Roman writers often remarked on: the Druids, the priests of the Celts, were interested in the ideas of Pythagoras.
Remember where these objects were found. Gaul and Britain. Celtic lands. Places where Celts and Romans met.
So in this view, the dodecahedron wasn't a tool at all. It was a symbol, or something used in a ritual, shaped by a philosophy that traveled from Greece to the Celtic world.
It would explain why they were expensive. Why they were polished. Why they show so little wear. And why no farmer, soldier, or builder ever wrote about them.
But it's important to be clear. This is still a theory. It's a well-argued one, but no one has found a text that says, this is what the dodecahedron was for.
So let's put it all together.
More than a hundred bronze dodecahedrons. Twelve faces, holes of different sizes, a knob on every corner.
Made with care, mostly in Gaul, between the second and fourth centuries.
Found from Britain to Hungary, but never in Italy.
Not a single Roman description. More than fifty theories.
Dice that won't roll. A rangefinder without markings. A knitting tool a thousand years too early. A candle holder that's far too complicated.
And a newer idea that it may have been a sacred symbol, connected to Pythagoras and the Druids.
Long ago, someone knew exactly what this was for. Today, nobody does.
And the next answer might come from a field in England, dug up by people who just like to look.
